T1A01: Part of ham radio's stated purpose: advancing skills in the technical and communication sides of radio. It's a hobby for learning, not a public phone service.
T1A02: The FCC regulates and enforces amateur radio in the US. The ARRL is a club, not a regulator.
T1A03: Phonetics are encouraged for phone ID, not required.
T1A04: New licenses arrive as an email from the FCC with a link to download the license. No paper in the mail.
T1A05: You're licensed once you appear in the FCC ULS database. The exam paperwork (CSCE) isn't the license.
T1A07: A space station is any amateur station more than 50 km above the Earth.
T1A08: Repeater channels are recommended by a volunteer frequency coordinator recognized by local hams. No FCC involvement.
T1A09: Local and regional hams who could run repeaters choose the frequency coordinator.
T1A10: To be a RACES control operator, you need certification of enrollment in a civil defense organization.
T1A11: Willful or malicious interference is prohibited. International VHF contacts and digital third-party traffic are fine.
T1B02: Any Technician or higher can work the ISS on VHF.
T1B03: 6 m runs 50-54 MHz, so 52.525 MHz is in it (a popular FM simplex frequency).
T1B04: 2 m runs 144-148 MHz. 146.52 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency.
T1B05: Technicians can use digital modes like FT8 on all three: 10, 6, and 2 m.
T1B07: CW-only segments: 50.0-50.1 MHz and 144.0-144.1 MHz, the bottom 100 kHz of 6 and 2 m.
T1B08: Where hams are secondary, primary users have priority. You must avoid interfering with them.
T1B09: All three reasons to stay off the exact band edge: display calibration error, sidebands spilling over, and drift.
T1B10: Above 50 MHz, SSB is allowed in at least part of every band.
T1B11: Technician HF power limit: 200 W PEP.
T1B12: Above 30 MHz, Technicians can run the full 1500 W PEP.
T1C01: New licenses today: Technician, General, Extra. Novice and Advanced are no longer issued.
T1C02: Any licensed amateur can apply for a vanity call sign.
T1C03: International contacts: only things incidental to amateur radio, plus personal remarks. No business.
T1C04: The FCC must be able to reach you by email. If it can't, your license can be revoked or suspended.
T1C05: Group D (Technician/General) format is 2 letters, a number, 3 letters: KF1XXX.
T1C06: On a US-documented vessel in international waters, you can operate with the master's permission.
T1C07: You can request renewal up to 90 days before your license expires.
T1C09: Grace period after expiration: 2 years to renew.
T1C10: Your first license: you can transmit once your grant appears in the FCC database, not when you leave the exam.
T1C11: An expired license means no transmitting, even in the grace period, until it's renewed.
T1D01: Contacts are banned only with countries that have notified the ITU they object.
T1D02: Broadcasting (sending to the general public) is prohibited. Code practice, event announcements, and telemetry are fine.
T1D03: Encoding to obscure meaning is allowed only for control commands to space stations or model craft.
T1D04: Music is allowed only when it's incidental to retransmitting manned spacecraft communications.
T1D05: You can mention ham gear for sale or trade, as long as it's amateur equipment and not done regularly.
T1D06: Any indecent or obscene language is prohibited. There's no official word list.
T1D07: Auxiliary station example: the one-way link from a remote repeater receiver to the main repeater transmitter.
T1D08: Paid operation is allowed for teachers: when the communication is part of classroom instruction.
T1D09: You can support news gathering only for the immediate safety of human life or protection of property, when no other means is available.
T1D10: Broadcasting = transmissions meant for the general public.
T1D11: Model craft control signals don't need ID. Everything else does.
T1D12: Test transmissions still need station ID.
T1E01: A station never transmits without a control operator. Even a repeater has one.
T1E02: Through a satellite, the control operator can be any ham allowed to transmit on the uplink frequency.
T1E03: The station licensee designates the control operator.
T1E04: Frequency privileges follow the control operator's license class.
T1E05: Control point = where the control operator actually performs the control function.
T1E06: A Technician can never control a station on Extra-only frequencies (except in an emergency).
T1E07: When the control operator isn't the licensee, both of them are responsible.
T1E09: Any station may be remotely controlled.
T1E10: Remote control example: running the station over the internet.
T1E11: Control operator: the ham the licensee designates as responsible for transmissions and rule compliance.
T1F01: An FCC representative can inspect the station and its records at any time, on request.
T1F02: Even with tactical calls, give your FCC call sign at least every 10 minutes and at the end.
T1F03: ID at least every 10 minutes during a contact, and at the end of it.
T1F04: Phone ID must be in English.
T1F05: Phone stations ID using CW or phone.
T1F06: All of these work on phone: stroke, slant, and slash all mean the / in a call sign.
T1F07: A non-licensed person can talk to a foreign station only if that country has a third-party agreement with the US.
T1F08: Third-party communication = a message passed between control operators on behalf of someone else.
T1F09: A repeater simultaneously retransmits a signal on another channel.
T1F10: If a repeater passes along a rule violation, the originating station's control operator is accountable.
T1F11: A club station license requires at least four members.
